message.content:
In Ancient Greek the person who **establishes laws and orders** is called a **law‑giver** – *νόμοθεκὴς* (*nomothekēs*).  
The verb “to establish” is *θεσπίζω* (*thespizō*), so you could say:

> **Ποιος θεσπίζει νόμους και τάξεις;**  
> *Poios thespizō nomous kai taxis?*  
> “Who establishes laws and orders?”

Some of the most famous Greek law‑givers were:

| Law‑giver | Period / City | Notable Contributions |
|-----------|---------------|-----------------------|
| **Δράκων (Drakon)** | 7th c. BCE, Athens | First codified Athenian laws (very harsh). |
| **Σόλων (Solon)** | 6th c. BCE, Athens | Reformed Athenian constitution, reduced debt slavery. |
| **Λύκουργος (Lycurgus)** | 8th–7th c. BCE, Sparta | Established Spartan military‑theocratic state. |
| **Θέμιστος (Themistocles)** | 5th c. BCE, Athens | Naval reforms, Athenian democracy. |
| **Πολύβιος (Polybius)** | 2nd c. BCE, Rome (Greek historian) | Analyzed Greek political systems. |

These figures are often referred to as *νόμοθεκὴς* in classical texts.
